writtenBy: Words: Brewster M. Higley. Music: Daniel E. Kelley
aboutKids: A happy song about a cozy home on wide, open grassland, with buffalo, deer and antelope nearby and big, clear skies above.
story: Brewster Higley, a doctor homesteading in Kansas, wrote the poem 'My Western Home' in the early 1870s, and his friend Daniel Kelley set it to music. Cowboys and settlers carried it west. When a 1934 lawsuit claimed the song, investigators traced it back to Higley. Kansas made it the state song in 1947.
funFact: Higley's little log cabin in Kansas, where the song was written, still stands and is listed on the National Register of Historic Places.
catalogNote: The Kansas Historical Society dates the earliest documented printings to 1874 (Kirwin Chief, March 1874; Smith County Pioneer early that year). Other sources say 1873, so the catalog's 1873 should be read as 1873 or 1874.

writtenBy: Words: Isaac Watts. Tune: 'Antioch', arranged by Lowell Mason
aboutKids: A bright, bouncy Christmas song that invites the whole wide world, the fields, hills and seas, to sing and celebrate together.
story: Isaac Watts wrote the words in 1719 as a retelling of Psalm 98 in his book The Psalms of David Imitated; it was not written specifically for Christmas. American music teacher Lowell Mason matched it with the tune 'Antioch' in the 1830s, and the pairing became a Christmas favorite in North America.
funFact: It is the most-published Christmas hymn in North America, appearing in more than 1,300 hymnals.
myth: Often said to be by Handel. The tune has never been found in Handel's works; Mason labelled it 'arranged from Handel' because a few phrases resemble Messiah, but scholars treat it as Mason's own arrangement of an American tune.
catalogNote: Mason first paired this tune with Watts's words in Occasional Psalm and Hymn Tunes (1836); his 1839 Modern Psalmist version, cited in the catalog, is a later, very similar printing. The date of the arrangement is better given as 1836-1839.

writtenBy: Traditional; first published by Charles E. Pratt (as H. J. Fuller)
origin: Uncertain; British Isles roots, popularized in the United States
aboutKids: Someone misses a dear friend who sailed far away across the big blue ocean, and wishes with all their heart they would come home.
story: Nobody knows who first wrote it. Shoppers were asking for it in music stores in the 1870s, so Charles E. Pratt published it in 1881 as 'Bring Back My Bonnie to Me' under a pen name. It became a hit with college singing groups, and may grow from an 1860s stage song, 'My Barney Lies over the Ocean'.
funFact: In 1961 the Beatles recorded it in Hamburg backing singer Tony Sheridan, one of their very first records.
myth: Often said to be a secret song about Bonnie Prince Charlie after 1746. This is only a guess: no early source links the song to him, and the first known printing is from 1881.
catalogNote: The catalog calls it a 'Scottish folk song', but no Scottish source has been found. Folklorists point to an 1860s English/Irish stage song ('My Barney Lies over the Ocean') reworked by American college singers in the 1880s; best described as traditional, origin uncertain.

writtenBy: Traditional American; credited to Percy Montrose
aboutKids: A gold miner's daughter named Clementine wears very big shoes, and her sweetheart sings about how much he misses his darling.
story: The familiar version was published in Boston in 1884 and credited to Percy Montrose, about whom nothing else is known. An 1863 song with similar words but a different tune came earlier, and another version appeared in 1885. Set in Gold Rush mining country, it became a mock-sad campfire favorite.
funFact: It was the signature song of the cartoon dog Huckleberry Hound, who sang it in his own wobbly, mixed-up way.
catalogNote: Consistent with the catalog. Note that authorship is uncertain: the 1863 'Down by the River Liv'd a Maiden' (credited to H. S. Thompson) and an 1885 version credited to Barker Bradford also exist.

writtenBy: Joseph Brackett (attributed)
aboutKids: A gentle, happy song about keeping things simple, being kind, and turning round and round until you land in just the right spot.
story: Elder Joseph Brackett, a member of the Shakers, a religious community known for plain living, is credited with the song around 1848 in Alfred, Maine. Shakers sang it while dancing. It became famous worldwide after Aaron Copland used it in the 1944 ballet Appalachian Spring.
funFact: Shaker songbooks call it a quick dance, and the song's words about turning were actually instructions for the dancers' steps.

writtenBy: French words and tune: Traditional (anonymous). English words: James Chadwick
year: Early 19th century (first printed 1805 or 1842); English words 1860-62
aboutKids: In this Christmas carol, shepherds out in the fields hear angels singing high in the sky, and the happy singing echoes over the hills.
story: This French carol, 'Les Anges dans nos campagnes', was sung by ordinary people long before anyone knew who wrote it. It was printed in France in the early 1800s. James Chadwick, a Catholic bishop in northern England, wrote the English words around 1860-62, and the carol has been sung across the English-speaking world ever since.
funFact: In the chorus, the single word Gloria is stretched across sixteen notes that climb up and tumble down, like a musical rollercoaster.
catalogNote: The catalog's '18th century' is not documented: the earliest known printings are 1805 (Wikipedia) or 1842 (Hymnology Archive, Choix de cantiques, Paris). Chadwick's English text was first printed in 1860 (Holy Family Hymns) and appeared revised in 1862 (The Crown of Jesus).

writtenBy: Music: Jacques Offenbach. English words: Little Duet
aboutKids: A super-fast, bouncy dance tune that makes you want to kick your legs up high and spin around until you giggle.
story: Jacques Offenbach wrote this whirlwind 'Galop infernal' as the closing dance of his comic operetta Orpheus in the Underworld, which opened in Paris in 1858 and was a huge hit. Decades later, Paris dance halls such as the Moulin Rouge adopted it for the high-kicking cancan, and the name stuck.
funFact: Offenbach never called it the Can-Can. The cancan dance already existed, and the tune only became its theme song years after he died.
myth: Often said that Offenbach invented the cancan or wrote this as cancan music. The dance began in Paris dance halls in the 1830s, and the tune was linked to it only in the 1890s.

writtenBy: Tune: Traditional Welsh ('Nos Galan'). English words: Thomas Oliphant
aboutKids: Everyone decorates the house with shiny green holly, gathers around, and sings a cheerful, silly chorus together.
story: The tune comes from 'Nos Galan', a Welsh song for New Year's Eve. It appears in an 18th-century manuscript by the harpist John Parry and was printed in 1794. Scottish writer Thomas Oliphant wrote new English words, not a translation, for an 1862 book of Welsh melodies, turning it into a Christmas favorite.
funFact: It started as a Welsh New Year's Eve song, and the English title said 'Hall', just one, until about the 1890s.
myth: Often said that Mozart used the tune in a violin sonata. This rests on a newspaper column and has not been confirmed; Haydn did arrange the tune in 1803.
catalogNote: The catalog's '16th century' is a traditional claim without documentary support; the earliest written source is John Parry's 18th-century manuscript, and the first printing with words is Edward Jones's Musical and Poetical Relicks of the Welsh Bards (1794).

writtenBy: Music: Ludwig van Beethoven. English words: Little Duet
aboutKids: A gentle piano tune that rocks back and forth like a little wave, written as a musical gift for a special friend.
story: Beethoven wrote this short piano piece in Vienna in 1810. It was never published in his lifetime: scholar Ludwig Nohl found it and printed it in 1867, forty years after Beethoven died. The manuscript Nohl saw has since been lost, so nobody can check the dedication, and it became one of the world's best-known piano tunes.
funFact: In Taiwan, garbage trucks play Fur Elise as they drive through neighborhoods, so families know it is time to bring out the rubbish.
myth: Often stated as fact that 'Elise' was Therese Malfatti, whose name Nohl misread. This is only one theory; others suggest the singer Elisabeth Rockel, and the manuscript is lost, so Elise's identity is unknown.

writtenBy: Traditional English tune (composer unknown)
aboutKids: A slow, dreamy old tune about a lovely lady who wore a dress with bright green sleeves.
story: In September 1580 a London printer, Richard Jones, registered a ballad called 'A Newe Northen Dittye of ye Ladye Greene Sleves', and the tune quickly became a hit, with more ballads written to it within a year. Shakespeare mentions it in The Merry Wives of Windsor, and in 1865 it became the Christmas carol 'What Child Is This?'
funFact: Shakespeare liked it enough to mention it twice in his comedy The Merry Wives of Windsor, written around 1597.
myth: Often said that King Henry VIII wrote it, sometimes for Anne Boleyn. Henry died in 1547, and the tune is built in an Italian style that reached England only after his death; it first appears in 1580.

writtenBy: Words: Charles Wesley (altered by George Whitefield). Music: Felix Mendelssohn, adapted by William H. Cummings
aboutKids: A joyful Christmas carol where angels sing happy news across the sky, and everyone on earth joins in the singing.
story: Charles Wesley wrote a 'Hymn for Christmas-Day' in 1739, and preacher George Whitefield rewrote its opening in 1753. The tune comes from a piece Felix Mendelssohn wrote in 1840 for a festival in Leipzig. In 1855 English organist William Cummings fitted Wesley's words to Mendelssohn's music, creating the carol sung today.
funFact: Mendelssohn wrote the tune to celebrate the 400th anniversary of the printing press, and said it would never suit religious words.
catalogNote: Consistent with the catalog. Cummings made the adaptation in 1855; Hymnary.org dates it to 1856, probably the year it was first published.

writtenBy: Music: Edvard Grieg. English words: Little Duet
aboutKids: A sneaky tiptoe tune from a fairy-tale mountain hall that starts slow and quiet, then gets faster and louder until everyone is racing.
story: Norwegian composer Edvard Grieg wrote this music in 1875 for Henrik Ibsen's play Peer Gynt, which opened in Christiania (now Oslo) in 1876. It plays when Peer finds himself in the hall of the troll king. The short theme repeats again and again, speeding up each time. Grieg later placed it in his first Peer Gynt Suite (1888).
funFact: Grieg himself did not like it: he wrote that it was so full of cowpats and Norwegian-ness that he could not bear to hear it.
catalogNote: Grieg's original is in B minor; the catalog's A minor is a transposition for the app, not the original key. The play with this music premiered on 24 February 1876.

writtenBy: Music: Christian Petzold. English words: Little Duet
aboutKids: A polite, graceful dance tune, made for bowing, stepping and twirling slowly with a partner.
story: Christian Petzold, an organist in Dresden, wrote this minuet as part of a harpsichord suite. It was copied into the music notebook Johann Sebastian Bach gave his wife Anna Magdalena in 1725, so for about 250 years everyone thought Bach wrote it. Research by Hans-Joachim Schulze, published around 1980, identified Petzold.
funFact: In 1965 the pop group The Toys turned it into a hit song called 'A Lover's Concerto', which reached number two in America.
myth: Widely called 'Bach's Minuet in G'. It is by Christian Petzold; Bach's notebook simply contained a copy.
catalogNote: The catalog's 'Written 1725' is really the date it was copied into the Anna Magdalena Bach notebook; Petzold's suite may date from around 1720.

writtenBy: Traditional American (author unknown)
aboutKids: A silly, happy singalong full of funny nonsense words, sung all day long on a trip to visit a friend.
story: No one knows who wrote it. It probably began on the 19th-century American minstrel stage as a 'walk-around', a finale where each performer sang a verse, and was popular around the 1860s. The first known printing is in Students' Songs, a Harvard songbook from 1880. It later became a children's singalong.
funFact: Its tune was borrowed for the 1979 Boney M. pop hit 'Hooray! Hooray! It's a Holi-Holiday'.
myth: Often credited to minstrel songwriter Dan Emmett, but there is no real evidence that he wrote it.
catalogNote: Consistent with the catalog. Wikipedia claims an 1843 premiere by Emmett's Virginia Minstrels, but the Traditional Tune Archive treats Emmett's authorship as unproven and names the 1880 Harvard book (ed. William H. Hills) as perhaps the first printing.

writtenBy: Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart
aboutKids: A bouncy, marching tune that sounds like a parade band coming down the street with booming drums and jingly bells.
story: Mozart wrote this as the last movement of his Piano Sonata in A major, K. 331, around 1783, and it was published in Vienna in 1784. Viennese audiences loved anything Turkish, and the music imitates the drums and cymbals of Ottoman Janissary military bands. It is now one of Mozart's best-known tunes.
funFact: Some pianos around 1800 had a special Janissary pedal that rang a bell and thumped like a drum, and pianists used it in this piece.

writtenBy: Words: Joseph Mohr. Music: Franz Xaver Gruber. English words: John Freeman Young
aboutKids: A soft, sleepy Christmas lullaby about a calm, quiet, starry night when a tiny baby is born.
story: Joseph Mohr, a young priest, wrote the words in 1816. In 1818 he asked schoolteacher Franz Xaver Gruber for a tune with guitar accompaniment, and they first sang it on Christmas Eve at St Nicholas Church in Oberndorf. Travelling folk singers spread it across Europe, and John Freeman Young's 1859 English version is the one most sung today.
funFact: Silent Night has been translated into about 300 languages, and Austria lists it as part of its cultural heritage with UNESCO.
myth: Often said mice chewed the church organ, so the song was written for guitar. There is no evidence of mice; the organ may have been damaged by flooding, and the broken-organ story was popularized by a fictional 1930s American tale.
catalogNote: Mohr wrote the words in 1816 (confirmed by a manuscript found in 1995), not 1818. The song was first performed in 1818 but first printed in 1833 (Four Genuine Tyrolean Songs), so 'Published 1818' should read 'first performed 1818'.

writtenBy: Johann Strauss II
aboutKids: A swirly, twirly waltz that sounds like a big river flowing along while dancers spin round and round.
story: Johann Strauss II, Vienna's 'Waltz King', wrote it in 1866 as a piece for a men's choir, first sung in Vienna in February 1867. He then turned it into an orchestral piece for the 1867 Paris World's Fair, where it became a sensation. It is now a beloved symbol of Austria, played at Vienna's New Year's concerts.
funFact: Composer Johannes Brahms once signed a fan with its opening notes and wrote 'Unfortunately not by Johannes Brahms'.
myth: Often said the first performance was a flop. Vienna newspapers at the time called it a hit, though the choral premiere was a more modest success than the orchestral version later in Paris.
catalogNote: Strauss composed it in 1866; 1867 is the year of the premiere and publication. Otherwise consistent.

writtenBy: Georges Bizet
aboutKids: A proud, bold march for a brave hero who strides in while the whole crowd cheers, claps and waves.
story: Georges Bizet wrote it for his opera Carmen, set in Spain, which opened in Paris on 3 March 1875. It is the entrance song of Escamillo, a famous bullfighter. Early audiences were unsure about the opera, and Bizet died that June, before it became a worldwide success. Carmen is now among the most performed operas.
funFact: Bizet never visited Spain, even though Carmen is set there and is full of Spanish-style dances.

writtenBy: Traditional American fiddle tune
aboutKids: A fast, toe-tapping fiddle tune for stomping, clapping and square dancing in a big wooden barn.
story: The tune was first printed around 1834 as 'Zip Coon', a minstrel-show song whose original lyrics mocked Black Americans. In 1861 performer Dan Bryant published 'Turkey in de Straw', ending with this melody, and the new name stuck. It became a favorite of fiddlers and square dances, usually played without words.
funFact: Mickey Mouse plays this tune in Steamboat Willie (1928), one of the first cartoons with sound matched to the pictures.
catalogNote: Consistent with the catalog. Authorship of 'Zip Coon' is disputed (George Washington Dixon, Bob Farrell and George Nichols all claimed it), and the tune may draw on older British or Irish airs.

writtenBy: Traditional Anglo-American (author unknown)
origin: British North America (now the United States)
aboutKids: A silly marching song about a man who rides his pony into town and sticks a feather in his hat to look fancy.
story: The tune is older than the words. British soldiers sang early verses during the wars of the 1750s and 1760s to tease colonial American troops as country bumpkins. During the American Revolution, Americans adopted the song with their own verses and sang it proudly, and it has been an American favorite ever since.
funFact: In the 1770s, 'macaroni' did not mean pasta. It was slang for a flashy, very fashionable young man.
myth: Often said British army surgeon Richard Shuckburgh wrote it in New York around 1755. This is a popular story, but it is unproven, and the early dates are disputed.
catalogNote: The catalog says 1760s-1770s; the earliest verses may date to the mid-1750s (1755 or 1758 are often given), so '1750s-1770s' is safer.
